entries.note: Pokorny IEW p.53 heads the entry exactly 'apo (po, ap-u, pu) ‚ab, weg‘' and runs it to p.55, so four of Nourai's five variants (Apo, Apu, Pu 3, Pô 1), the language label and the gloss 'off' are literally Pokorny's; Walde-Pokorny I 47ff. and Watkins/AHD 'apo-. Also ap-. Off, away' agree. The one addition is 'Apâ' with long ā, which is not in Pokorny, WP, Watkins or Mann, and it is the peg on which Nourai hangs the whole ā- branch (nodes #6-#9). Old Iranian/Indo-Iranian ā 'to, toward' (Skt. ā́, Av./OP ā) is a separate particle (PIE *ē/*ō, Wiktionary *h₂ed), not an ablaut grade of *apo-; Horn (Grundriss no.1) and Cheung both handle it as an independent preverb. Hence the root box is right but over-extended, and everything under 'Apâ' has to be judged separately. A second cross-cutting problem: Nourai's BQT:1086 (cited on nodes #1, #6, #7) falls in the س- section of Borhān-e Qāţeʿ vol. 2 and has nothing to do with apa/ā, and KLN:168 on node #8 is Klein's 'behemoth–beige' page — almost certainly a slip for KNT:168, which does carry apadāna-.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaf 61 (= printed p.53): 'apo (po, ap-u, pu) ‚ab, weg‘ — Ai. ápa ‚weg, fort, zurück‘ … av. ap. apa ‚von-weg‘ … gr. ἀπό … lat. ab …'; the entry continues 'po:' (p.54) and 'ap-u … pu' (p.55). Also on p.53: 'über privatives *ap- im Iran. und Gr. s. Schwyzer ZII. 6, 230ff.' — the privative that underlies node #2/#3. Exactly the root, language and gloss Nourai prints; only 'Apâ' is absent.

nodes.derivation: Avestan apa is the inherited continuant of PIE *apo 'off, away' with regular Iranian retention of the medial -p- (unlike Indic, which also keeps it: Skt. ápa). Bartholomae AiW col. 71-72 lists 'apa 1) Adv. ‚weg, getrennt von—‘ (nur Komp.) 2) Praev. (mit karət-, gaud-, gam-, bar-, yam-, štar- usw.)', i.e. it survives mainly as a preverb, which is exactly the use Nourai's daughter nodes need. The superlative is formed with PIE *-m⌥o-: *apo-mo- > Av. apəma- 'the last (in time)', and with the double superlative *-t̥mo- (Skt. -tama-) *apa-tama- > MIr. abdom. Nourai's added gloss 'to' for apa is wrong (apa is ablatival, 'away from'), and 'apatama' is a reconstruction, not an attested Avestan form.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian abē- (Book Pahlavi ʾPʿ(y)-, Manichaean ʾby-) 'without, -less' goes back to an Old Iranian instrumental/locative *apa-i ‘away from’ built on the preposition apa; Hübschmann sets it up as OP *apaiy from apa + i (like naiy 'not' = na + i), and notes that the form arose in composition, because a free *apaiy would have given NP āb. It is productive only as first member of compounds (abē-bīm 'fearless', abē-gumān 'certain', abē-niyāz 'free from want'). This is the standard modern account and matches Nourai's arrow Av. apa → Phlv. apē exactly.

nodes.derivation: New Persian بی bī- 'without' is the regular continuation of MP abē-: the initial a- of the unstressed prefix was lost in NP (MP abē-bīm > NP bī-bīm), the older stage surviving as ابی abē/ebē in early NP verse, which Nourai correctly prints in the box (ابی-) and Moʿin glosses 'بی: [= ابی] (پش.) علامت نفی و سلب'. That half is confirmed and is the standard view (Horn 247, Hübschmann 247, MacKenzie s.v. abē-, Wiktionary بی < ابی < MP apē < PIE *h₂epo); the compounds in the extras (بی‌نیاز، بی‌بهره، بی‌شمار) are all straightforward bī- privatives. The second word is the problem. بیدستر bīdastar 'beaver' is analysed by Moʿin (and before him by Borhān-e Qāţeʿ) as بی 'without' + دستر glossed 'داس کوچک، اره' — 'without a sickle/saw', i.e. an animal that fells trees with no tool. That is a transparent folk etymology of the Borhān type: دستر 'small sickle' is not otherwise attested, and the word has the variants ویدستر vidastar and بادستر bādastar (the latter in Moʿin's own entry), whose v-/bā- cannot come from the privative bī-. Wiktionary (tentatively) takes the first element to be *widʰu- 'wood, tree', giving a 'wood-eater/wood-cutter' compound; Horn, Hübschmann and Bartholomae treat the Iranian beaver word as Av. baβri- / MP bawrak (Horn no.181) and never connect bīdastar with bī-. So the node's first word is confirmed and its second is a folk etymology inherited from Nourai's source.

ref_check.note: Not online; its original, Horn no.247, supports the bī < apē half (quoted at node #2).

Moʿin does say what Nourai says, for both words. The page number could not be pinned in the 2-vol Adena OCR (no page markers), but the entries are verbatim as Nourai reports them — including the 'without a saw' gloss that modern etymology rejects.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian abdom / afdom (Book Pahlavi ʾp̄dwm, Manichaean ʾbdwm, Pāzand awadum) 'last, finally' continues Old Iranian *apa-tama-, the *-tama- superlative of apa 'away, behind' — the same formation as Avestan apəma- but with the longer suffix. Intervocalic *-t- after the labial gave the Book Pahlavi spelling with p/f, and the word was borrowed into Biblical Aramaic as ʾappetōm (Ezra 4:13). Nourai's two spellings afdom and awdum are exactly the Book Pahlavi and Pāzand readings the handbooks print.

nodes.derivation: NP آفدم āfdom 'last, at last' is MP abdom taken over into early New Persian; it is a rare, early word (Mojmal al-tawārīkh, Rūdakī, Abū Šukūr, Asadī), usually met in the frozen adverbial بافدم bāfdom = be + āfdom 'in the end', which is the form Nourai's extras and Rūdakī quotation give. Hübschmann's caveat is worth recording: phonologically one expects short a-, afdum, and Nöldeke suggested (ap. Hübschmann no.38) that the word was already obsolete in the earliest NP poets' day and was therefore mispronounced with ā-. The word died out and has no modern currency.

nodes.words: â 1; â-vare; â-gam; â-râd, â-râiti 1; apa-spar; â-kand
nodes.derivation: The words themselves are real: Av./OP ā is a preverb/preposition 'to, toward, hither' that combines with bar- (ā-bar- 'bring'), gam- (ā-gam- 'come'), rād-/rāta- (ā-rā- 'set in order'), kan- (ā-kan- 'fill up'). But its ancestry is not *apo-. Skt. ā́, Av./OP ā and Gk. ὦ go back to an independent particle (PIE *ē/*ō; Wiktionary reconstructs *h₂ed), and every specialist treatment keeps the two apart: Horn's very first entry lists NP ā- under 'ap. aw. phlv. ā; ai. ā́' with no reference to apa, Cheung files āfrīnāmi under '*fraiH (+ *ā-)', and Pokorny's own apo- entry (pp.53-55) contains no ā-. Nourai's Avestan box therefore hangs a different preverb on the *apo- root by way of the invented root variant 'Apâ'. The one genuinely apa- item in the box, apa-spar 'walk away from, entrust', is also mis-prefixed: the ancestor of MP abespurdan / NP sepārdan is *upa-spar- (Cheung) or *abi-spar- (MacKenzie's Manichaean ʾbyspwrd), not *apa-spar-. Hence: right words, wrong parent.

Used with vb. gaud- and in sbb. apadāna-, apa-niyāka-; with suffix in apatara-, apara-'. nodes.derivation: The edge itself is right: NP آ-/ا- is the direct continuation of the Old Iranian preverb ā, preserved fossilised in verbs whose Middle Persian ancestors already carried it — آوردن (< *ā-bar-), آمدن (< *ā-gam-), آراستن (< *ā-rād-ta-), آکندن (< *ā-kan-) — all four of which stand in Nourai's extras. The separate '-ā-' is the same particle in its adverbial/prepositional use, used to link a repeated noun: Horn's own examples her ā her and gird ā gird are precisely Nourai's برابر، دمادم، سراسر، گرداگرد type. The only defect is inherited from the parent box: the preverb goes back to PIE *ē/*ō (*h₂ed), not to *apo-; and اسپاردن in the extras belongs to *upa-spar-, not to ā-.

ref_check.note: See node #1: BQT vol. 2 leaf 543 (≈ p.1086) is the سبز- section; nothing on the prefix آ-.

nodes.derivation: Three separate problems. (a) apa-dāna- 'off place, secret room of a palace' is a genuine word with exactly Nourai's analysis — but it is Old Persian, not Avestan: Kent p.168 'apadāna- sb. ‚palace‘: from apa- + dāna- to root *dā-, cf. Skt. apadhā- ‚concealment‘, Gk. ἀποθήκη ‚storehouse‘', attested in Artaxerxes II's Susa and Hamadan inscriptions (D²Sa, A²Ha imam apadāna); Bartholomae's AiW apa- run has no such Avestan compound, and Nourai himself puts it (rightly) in the Old Persian box #12 as well. (b) ā-frīnāmi 'I praise/bless' is genuine Young Avestan (Y 11.15, Y 52.1, Yt 13.51 āfrīnənti) and ā-pərəta- 'battle' is a real ā + parət- 'to fight' formation — but both contain the preverb ā-, from PIE *ē/*ō, not *apo-. (c) 'ā-fritan to create' is not Avestan at all: it is the Middle Persian infinitive āfrītan (BMP ʾplyn-/ʾplyt-), as Horn's no.39 explicitly labels it ('phlv. āfrītan ‚schaffen‘'). So the box mixes an Old Persian noun, two Avestan ā- formations and one Middle Persian verb, and none of the ā- items descends from the root of the chart.

nodes.derivation: آفرین and آورد are inherited and confirmed. āfarīn 'praise, bravo' is the present stem of آفریدن < MP āfrīn-/āfrītan 'to bless, create' < Av. ā-frīnāmi, PIE *preiH-; the antonym نفرین nifrīn < MP nifrīn 'curse' (*ni-frī-) and the agent آفریدگار in Nourai's extras belong to the same family. āvard 'combat' is the Shahnameh word (آوردگاه 'battlefield', آوردیدن), from ā- + parət- 'to fight', the exact counterpart of نبرد neberd < *ni-parət- (Horn no.1025); it must be kept apart from the homograph آورد 'he brought' (< ā-bar-). آپادانا is different in kind: it is not an inherited Persian word but a 20th-century learned re-borrowing of Old Persian apadāna from the Achaemenid inscriptions and archaeological literature (the Apadana of Persepolis/Susa); and its source is the Old Persian box #12, not an Avestan one. Hence 'plausible': two words confirmed, one with a mis-drawn parent and a learned rather than inherited transmission.

ref_check.note: Kent p.168 (KNT.txt leaf 190) gives 'apadāna- sb. ‚palace‘: from apa- + dāna- … For development in later Iranian, with āpa- by secondary lengthening … see Henning, TPS 1944.110n' — which is the source of Nourai's spelling āpādānā and supports that word. Kent says nothing about āfarīn or āvard.

nodes.derivation: Arabic عِفْريت ʿifrīt (vulgar ʿafrīt), a powerful demon; Qurʾanic (Q 27:39 ʿifrītun min al-jinn), whence English afreet. Asbaghi and Wiktionary both make it a Middle Iranian loan: from the past participle āfrīd 'created' (MP āfrītan/āfrīd-, the very verb of Nourai's parent box), originally elliptical for *dēw āfrīd 'a demon's creature' — which is exactly the chart's gloss 'demon creature'. The vocalisation ʿifrīt with initial ʿayn and the fiʿlīt shape are the usual Arabic adaptation of a foreign form to a native pattern. It is only 'plausible' because a purely internal Arabic derivation is also current: from the root ع-ف-ر 'dust, ashes' (cf. ʿafara 'to roll in the dust'), formed like عَكْرُوت ʿakrūt 'scoundrel'; Klein s.v. 'afreet' gives no Iranian source at all, and Jeffery's Foreign Vocabulary of the Qurʾān does not treat the word, i.e. he did not regard it as a loan.

nodes.derivation: Modern Persian عفریت ʿefrīt 'demon, fiend' (with the feminine عفریته ʿefrīte in the extras) is a straightforward Arabic loan back into Persian, taken over with its Arabic عاین spelling and its Arabic feminine in -a; Moʿin tags it '[ع.]' (Arabic). If Asbaghi and Wiktionary are right about node #10, this is a round trip: MP āfrīd → Arabic ʿifrīt → NP ʿefrīt, and the modern Persian word is thus unrelated in form to its own ancestor آفریدن, which is presumably why Nourai draws it as a separate Arabic-mediated branch. The borrowing is medieval and spread through Qurʾanic and 1001-Nights usage.

nodes.derivation: OP apa- and apadāna- are exactly right. Kent p.168: 'apa- prefix ‚away‘: Av. Skt. apa, Gk. ἀπό, Lt. ab, Gt. af, Gm. ab, NEng. of, off, pIE *apo. Used with vb. gaud- and in sbb. apadāna-, apa-niyāka-; with suffix in apatara-, apara-'; and 'apadāna- ‚palace‘: from apa- + dāna- to root *dā-, cf. Skt. apadhā- ‚concealment‘, Gk. ἀποθήκη ‚storehouse‘' — which is precisely Nourai's gloss 'off (secret) place' and his cross-reference to root Dhē 2 (*dheh₁-). Attested in A²Sa/A²Ha/D²Sa (imam apadāna(m)). The third item is the weak one: there is no Old Persian preposition pa or pō. Pokorny's 'po:' section (p.54) illustrates it from Avestan pa-zdayeiti, Latin pō-situs/pōnō, Albanian pa, Old High German fona and Slavic/Baltic po — not from Old Persian, and Kent's lexicon has no such entry.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaves 61-63 = pp.53-55 cover apo / po / ap-u / pu, including 'av. ap. apa ‚von-weg‘'. But the 'po:' paragraph on p.54 lists 'av. pa-zdayeiti ‚lässt wegrücken‘; lat. po-situs, pōnō … alb. pa … afries. fān … aksl. po' — no Old Persian pa/pō, so that word of the box is not supported by the cited pages.
KNT.txt leaf 190 (printed p.168) carries 'apa- prefix (§206b) ‚away‘ … pIE *apo' and 'apadāna- sb. ‚palace‘: from apa- + dāna-', i.e. two of the box's three words verbatim.

consulted.note: Bartholomae marks the Old Persian forms with 'p.' in the same apa- article, e.g. 'p. apataram Adv. 1) ‚abseits, anderswo‘ … 2) mit hacā ‚ausser‘'.
'apo (apo, apo, po) ‚away; from, after‘ … OCS po … Li. po' — Mann too attaches po to Slavic/Baltic, not to Old Persian.
'7. Possible root *po(s), on, in: a. Russian po … b. Latin post … c. Latin pōnere' — Watkins likewise gives the po- variant no Iranian, let alone Old Persian, reflex.

nodes.derivation: Three of the five are solid Old Persian: apara- 'later, after' (Kent p.168, apa- + comparative -ra-, asn. adverb aparam DB 4.37 etc.), apataram 'farther off, elsewhere' (nsn. of apatara- = apa- + -tara-, DNa 18, DSe 16f, XPb 25, XPh 16, cf. Gk. ἀπωτέρω), and apaniyāka- 'great-great-grandfather' (apa- + niyāka- 'grandfather', cf. Lat. abavus; A²Sa 3), where Nourai's gloss 'ancestors' is loose but the formation is Kent's. The other two fail. 'apa-had ‚put away‘' is unattested: Old Persian uses apa- with gaud- (apagaudaya- 'conceal', DB 4.54-57), and the root *had- 'sit' appears only in ni-šad-/niyašādayam (Kent, Cheung s.v. *had) — neither Kent nor Bartholomae nor Cheung has an *apa-had-. 'pan-s-dau ‚after that‘' is not Old Persian at all but OLD PRUSSIAN: it comes straight out of the page Nourai cites, Pokorny p.54, 'Eine ähnliche Form sucht Trautmann Apr. 389 in apr. pan-s-dau ‚danach‘' — where apr. = altpreußisch. Nourai evidently read the abbreviation as 'Old Persian'. The book page (pdf 59) does print it inside the Old Persian box, so this is the author's error, not a scan artefact.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaf 62 (= p.54, within the cited range): 'Eine ähnliche Form sucht Trautmann Apr. 389 in apr. pan-s-dau ‚danach‘' — apr. = Old Prussian, in the Baltic part of the 'po' paragraph. Pokorny does support ap. apataram ('ap. apataram Adv. ‚abseits, anderswo‘', p.54) and av./ap. apara-, but he flatly contradicts the Old Persian label on pan-s-dau, and has no apa-had.

Kent p.168 (leaf 190) has 'apataram adv. ‚farther off, far off‘ … DNa 18; DSe 16f; XPb 25; XPh 16', 'apara- adj. ‚later, after‘ … aparam asn. as adv. DB 4.37 …', 'apaniyāka- sb. ‚great-great-grandfather‘: from apa- + niyāka- ‚grandfather‘, cf. Lt. ab-avos … A²Sa 3' — three of five. It has neither apa-had nor pan-s-dau; for *had- it offers only 'pIE *sed- ‚sit‘, OP had-iš ‚seat, abode‘' and the causative ni-šādaya-.

consulted.note: For the apa- verb Kent gives only apa-gaud-: 'inj. 2sg. … apa-gaudaya (DB 4.54)', 'mā … apagaudaya' — the Old Persian apa- verb is 'conceal', not 'put away'.
Cheung lists the preverbs attested with *had as *abi- and *ni- only ('OLD PERSIAN: (+ *ni-) ni-sad- (caus.) ‚to establish‘ … niyašādayam'); no *apa-had- anywhere in Iranian.
'apo-teros ‚further, following‘. WP I, 47 … Skt. OPer. apataram; Gk. apóteros; Go. aftaro' — independent confirmation of the Old Persian apataram.

nodes.derivation: The compound is real but is a reconstruction, and 'Old Iranian' rather than specifically Old Persian is the right label: Nyberg sets up MP apārōn < OIr *apārda-van-, formed with the suffix -van- from *apārda- < *apa-arda- 'whose side is turned away' (apa- 'away' + arda- 'side, half', the same *ardha- as in Skt. árdha- 'half, side'). The mirror-image compound *frārda-van- > MP frārōn 'righteous, upright' (< *fra-arda- 'whose side is turned forward') guarantees the analysis. No such word is attested in the Achaemenid inscriptions, so Kent has nothing; Kent's OP arda- is a different word, 'light' (ardata- 'silver', ardastāna-).

ref_check.note: Pokorny pp.53-55 give the apo- root and its derivatives apo-tero-, ap-ero-, ap-io-, ap-ōko-, but there is no apa-ardha compound on those pages; the compound has to be got from Nyberg (node #15) or from Pokorny's separate *ardh- article.

nodes.derivation: Middle Persian abārōn (Book Pahlavi ʾpʾlʹlwnʹ/ʾpʾlwnʹ) 'contrary, wrong, perverse, sinful', adverbially 'backward' (= abāz), Pāzand āwārūn, is the regular outcome of *apārda-van-: the cluster *-rd- gives Middle Persian -r-/-l- in the Book Pahlavi orthography, and the suffix *-āna-/-ōn is the same as in its antonym frārōn 'righteous'. The word is a technical term of Zoroastrian moral vocabulary, abārōnīh meaning 'sin' and being the standing opposite of frārōnīh.

Both of Nourai's glosses ('wrong, upside down') and the whole three-box chain are here.

nodes.derivation: NP وارون vārūn 'upside down, inverted, perverse' (with the extended وارونه vārūne of the extras) is inherited directly from MP abārōn: initial ab-/aw- regularly yields NP wā-/vā- (cf. MP abāz > NP باز/واز), so *abārōn > wārūn. Classical Persian keeps the moral sense of the Pahlavi word ('wicked, ill-omened, بخت وارون ‚ill fortune‘'), while modern Persian has generalised the physical sense 'inverted'. The word was borrowed onward into Ottoman Turkish as varun.

nodes.derivation: Latin ab 'from, away from' (governing the ablative) is the direct Italic reflex of PIE *apo: intervocalic/pre-voiced *-p- was voiced to -b-, the older *ap surviving in aperiō < *ap-weriō and in the by-forms abs (before c, t: abstineō, abscondō), as- (before p: asportō), and ā- (before m, u, b: āmoveō, āvellō, ābitō). Cognate with Gk. ἀπό, Skt. ápa, Goth. af, OE of/off. Nourai's gloss 'away' and the language label are correct.

nodes.derivation: English abnormal (17th c.) is a Latinate formation whose first element is the Latin preposition/prefix ab- of node #17: Klein describes it as a blend of Latin abnormis 'deviating from a rule' (ab + norma 'carpenter's square, rule') with Medieval Latin anormalis, itself a blend of Latin anomalus (< Gk. ἀνώμαλος) and normalis — which is why the earlier English form was anormal and why the -b- was restored on the model of Latin ab-. Only the prefix comes from *apo-; the stem is from PIE *ǵneh₃- 'to know' via Latin norma (Watkins indexes ABNORMAL under gnō-, and ABLAUT, AFTER, EBB, OF, OFF, AWKWARD under apo-). The empty ref field is correct — Nourai cites nothing for this box.
